claims.claim: Hong Kong should tighten limits on rent increases, give tenants three years of security of tenure, and move enforcement effort towards the condition of the flats.
Hong Kong should not cap starting rents.
About 110,000 households live in subdivided units.
Subdivided unit tenants pay 15 to 25 percent more per square foot than tenants in ordinary flats.
Subdivided unit tenants are often new arrivals, single parents, or people waiting for public housing.
The 2021 Tenancy Control Ordinance capped rent increases inside a tenancy but did not cap the starting rent.
The number of subdivided units grew from 107,300 in 2021 to 111,200 in 2025.
Rents per square foot rose more slowly under the law, 3.1 percent against 6.8 percent before it.
Rent burden still went from 31 to 34 percent of income.
Hard caps on rent levels show steady shrinking of supply, while caps on increases show small or no effects.
A model of a 15 percent cut in starting rents finds that people already inside gain about 900 dollars a month, but 3,000 to 4,000 households a year cannot get in, mostly new arrivals.
Berlin's rent cap helped those already inside and handed the bill to those still outside, and when a court struck it down, rents for new contracts jumped above the old trend.
Landlords say members will leave the market if returns fall below mortgage cost.
The landlords' association admits it has no data on its members' real margins, and its cost figures come from a self-reported survey with a 34 percent response rate.
Inspection covers under 6 percent of stock each year.
Tenants who have no written agreement or who are new are the least able to complain, so enforcement based on complaints would miss the most exploited.
The subcommittee could not find a design that protects the newest arrivals first.
A survey of 440 households found that 61 percent would accept a nominal rent rise for three years of security, and 74 percent would trade it for a faster public housing offer.
The report argues that caps treat the price symptom of a long queue, and that inspection effort is better spent on fire, partition and ventilation, where harm is documented.
A limit on rent increases is still needed because without one a landlord could end a secure tenancy by pricing the tenant out at renewal.
